title: The Story of Money
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Money seems so natural that it is hard to imagine life without it. Yet for most of human history, people lived without coins or notes, and they obtained what they needed by barter, that is, by exchanging goods directly. Barter has a serious weakness: it works only when each person has something that the other wants. A farmer with a spare sheep who needs shoes must find a shoemaker who happens to need a sheep. Economists call this the problem of the double coincidence of wants, and money was invented to solve it.

The earliest forms of money were ordinary objects that people agreed to accept. In different times and places, shells, salt, cattle, beads and bricks of tea have all been used. A good form of money must be easy to carry, hard to copy, divisible into small parts, and durable. Cattle fail the test of portability and shells the test of durability. Metals such as gold, silver and bronze met all the conditions, and by about 3000 BC, merchants in Mesopotamia were using weighed pieces of silver as a standard of value.

The first true coins were made in the kingdom of Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, around 600 BC. Each coin was a lump of a natural mixture of gold and silver, stamped with a picture to guarantee its weight and purity. The idea spread quickly. Greek cities issued their own coins, and the Romans, who built a huge empire, used coins to pay their soldiers and to collect taxes, so that the same money circulated from Britain to Syria.

Paper money appeared in China during the Tang and Song dynasties, as a convenient alternative to carrying heavy strings of copper coins. Merchants first left their coins with a trusted shop in return for a receipt, and the receipts began to be accepted in place of the coins. The government soon took control of the system and printed official notes. When the Italian traveller Marco Polo described this in the thirteenth century, many of his readers found it hard to believe that paper could be worth anything.

In Europe, the next great change came with banks. Merchants in Italian cities such as Florence and Venice held accounts for their customers and let them make payments by a written order, an ancestor of the cheque. Banks also discovered that most depositors did not ask for their money at the same time, so they could lend part of it out and charge interest. This practice made trade easier, but it created the risk of a bank run, in which many customers demand their money at once, and the bank fails.

In the twentieth century, money lost its last connection with precious metal. Until the 1970s, many countries promised that their notes could be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold. When they abandoned this promise, money came to depend only on trust in the government that issued it. Today most money exists only as numbers in computer systems; coins and notes make up a small part of the total in wealthy countries, and in some, a growing share of shops no longer accept cash.

The newest form of money is digital currency. Cryptocurrencies, of which Bitcoin is the best known, are not issued by any government; they are created and recorded by a network of computers. Supporters say that they offer freedom from control by banks. Critics reply that their prices change wildly, that they are used by criminals, and that the computers which create them consume huge amounts of electricity. Dr Lucia Ferraro, a monetary historian, believes that money will continue to change, as it has always done, but that trust will remain its foundation.
